table.text: Before the field period, participants completed a screening questionnaire (consent, eligibility, demographics, social-media use, past-year gambling, and the PGSI) and received illustrated instructions that defined messages about gambling broadly, from operator advertising to memes, betting tips, and anti-gambling messages.
Participants were recruited through the commercial online panel IPSOS, the university participant pool, and flyers.
One further participant completed no scheduled questionnaire after the first one and was excluded.
Participants completed 1,976 of 2,314 possible questionnaires after the first (compliance rate of 85.4%; M = 11.10 per person, Mdn = 12, range 1-13).

We had preregistered a target of at least 180 analysable participants, based on simulations of the planned mixed models that assumed about 2.5 reported encounters per participant per day, an intraclass correlation of .40, a within-person coefficient of about 0.15 for positive expectancies and urge, and an odds ratio of about 1.40 for gambling; under these assumptions, 180 participants were expected to provide a power of at least .80.
Each scheduled questionnaire asked whether participants had gambled since the last notification and, if so, for how many minutes in total and with what total stake in euros.
Participants had to stop what they were doing, take a screenshot, and upload it.

table.text: The final analytic sample thus comprised 178 participants aged 18-30 (M = 24.20, SD = 3.68); 109 identified as men, 68 as women, and one as nonbinary. In the past year, 87.1% had bet on sports online and 78.7% had played online casino games. Participants completed 1,976 of 2,314 possible questionnaires after the first (compliance rate of 85.4%; M = 11.10 per person, Mdn = 12, range 1-13). We had preregistered a target of at least 180 analysable participants, based on simulations of the planned mixed models that assumed about 2.5 reported encounters per participant per day, an intraclass correlation of .40, a within-person coefficient of about 0.15 for positive expectancies and urge, and an odds ratio of about 1.40 for gambling; under these assumptions, 180 participants were expected to provide a power of at least .80. Interactions with risk were not powered. The final sample fell slightly short of this target, and exposure was lower than assumed (about one documented encounter per participant per day rather than 2.5), which reduces the power of the within-person comparisons.

table.title: Everyday Gambling Marketing Exposure and Proximal Responses - 2026
table.existing_data_explanation: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
RQ1 In a tightly regulated Dutch market, what is the frequency of young adults' real-world exposure to gambling marketing across channels?

 H1 Within participants, intervals containing at least one recorded gambling-marketing exposure will be associated with higher perceived benefits of gambling at the next scheduled prompt (H1a), stronger momentary urge to gamble at the next scheduled prompt (H1b), and greater odds of gambling during the reporting interval (H1c), compared with classifiable intervals without recorded exposure.

 RQ2 To what extent do moderate/high-risk gamblers differ from no/low-risk gamblers in (a) the frequency of recorded gambling-marketing exposure and (b) the diversity and distribution of exposure channels?

 H2 Gambling-risk group will moderate the within-person association between exposure and outcomes. Compared with no/low-risk gamblers, moderate/high-risk gamblers will show larger exposed-versus-unexposed differences in perceived benefits (H2a), urge (H2b), and the odds of gambling during the reporting interval (H2c).
table.design_dependent_variables: The three primary prompt-level dependent variables are: (1) positive gambling expectancies, the mean of three 1–7 items following 'If I were to gamble now': I would have fun, come across as cool among friends and peers, and win money; the score is computed when all three items are present; (2) current urge to gamble, rated 0 (no desire) to 100 (overwhelming desire); and (3) any gambling since the previous scheduled prompt, coded 0 = no and 1 = yes. For RQ1/RQ2, participant-level outcomes are the number of valid exposure reports, exposure rate per valid observation day, number of distinct participant-reported channel categories, and channel-specific counts/proportions. Two negative expectancy items, money staked, and minutes gambled are secondary.
table.study_design_overview: Participants are not randomly assigned to conditions. This is an observational seven-day EMA. The time-varying within-person comparison is between classifiable intervals with at least one recorded gambling-marketing exposure and intervals without recorded exposure. The person-level grouping variable is baseline PGSI risk: no/low risk (0–2) versus moderate/high risk (3–27).
table.statistical_tests:
RQ1 will be addressed descriptively using valid event reports. We will report the total number of recorded exposures, exposures per participant and per valid observation day, the proportion of participants and participant-days with at least one exposure, and counts and percentages by participant-reported channel.

 For RQ2, participants will be classified as no/low risk (PGSI 0–2) or moderate/high risk (PGSI 3–27). Exposure frequency will be compared between groups using negative-binomial regression, with each participant's number of valid exposure reports as the outcome, risk group as the predictor, and the logarithm of valid observation days as an offset. Channel diversity and channel-specific exposure distributions will be summarized separately by risk group.

 For H1 and H2, valid event reports will be assigned to the first subsequent valid scheduled prompt. An interval will be coded as exposed if it contains at least one valid exposure report. It will be coded as unexposed if it contains no event report and the participant reports no gambling-marketing exposure during the preceding 60 minutes. Intervals with no event report but a positive recent-exposure response, or for which exposure timing cannot be established, will be classified as ambiguous and excluded from the confirmatory models.

 Exposure will be decomposed into each participant's mean exposure across classifiable intervals and a person-mean-centred interval-level exposure variable. Positive gambling expectancies and urge will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Gambling during the reporting interval will be analyzed using mixed-effects logistic regression. Models will include a participant random intercept, person-mean-centred exposure, person-level mean exposure, risk group, day index, time of day, weekend versus weekday, and hours since the preceding prompt.

 H1 will be tested using the coefficient for person-mean-centred exposure. H2 will be tested by adding the interaction between person-mean-centred exposure and risk group. We predict positive coefficients for the H1 exposure effects and the H2 interaction effects. All tests will be two-sided with alpha = .05, and estimates, 95% confidence intervals, and exact p values will be reported.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will exclude technical or researcher test accounts identified from administrative records, participants who withdrew consent or requested deletion of their data, and records from individuals who did not meet the study's eligibility criteria. If administrative records show that multiple participant IDs belong to the same individual, their records will be combined before applying the compliance criterion. Clearly duplicated submissions referring to the same exposure encounter will be counted as one event.

 The participant-level analytic sample will include participants who completed at least 10 of the 14 scheduled prompts. A scheduled prompt will be valid if it was completed within 120 minutes of the notification. An event report will be valid if it was submitted within 60 minutes of the reported exposure and the report or uploaded material can be verified as relating to gambling marketing. Reports concerning material unrelated to gambling marketing will not be counted as exposures. We will not require participants to report a minimum number of exposures.

 For the H1 and H2 models, we will include all valid scheduled prompts with a nonmissing outcome and classifiable exposure status from participants meeting the compliance criterion. Ambiguous exposure intervals will be excluded as described in Question 5. Participants or observations missing PGSI information will be excluded from analyses requiring risk-group classification.

 No outcome values will be removed or winsorized solely because they are statistically extreme. Values outside the programmed response ranges will be treated as missing after verification against the raw export. Missing outcomes will not be imputed; each model will use all observations with complete information for the variables included in that model. All exclusions and the numbers of affected participants and observations will be reported.

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
Data collection is complete, and no additional participants will be recruited. A total of 209 participants completed the first EMA questionnaire. The final analytic sample will include all participants who completed at least 10 of the 14 scheduled prompts. No minimum number of reported marketing exposures will be required. The final number of participants and prompt-level observations will therefore be determined by these prespecified compliance and observation-validity rules.

 The original target was at least 180 analyzable participants. This target was informed by simulations of the planned mixed-effects models. The planning assumptions included an average of approximately 2.5 reported marketing exposures per participant per day, an intraclass correlation of .40 for the continuous outcomes, a small within-person exposure coefficient of approximately b = 0.15 for perceived benefits and urge, an odds ratio of approximately 1.40 for interval gambling, and a two-sided alpha of .05. Under these assumptions, a sample of approximately 180 participants was expected to provide at least .80 power for the main within-person exposure association. Additional participants were recruited to allow for incomplete participation, invalid reports, and lower-than-expected exposure. The study was not specifically powered for the exposure-by-risk-group interaction; this interaction will therefore be interpreted with particular attention to its confidence interval and the numbers of exposed and unexposed observations in each risk group.

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
Data collection was completed before this registration was submitted. However, the authors had not examined any substantive questionnaire responses, descriptive results, associations, group differences, or hypothesis tests. We inspected only participant identifiers and completion-status information to determine the number of participants; no response values were viewed.

 The study design, measures, research questions, and hypotheses were specified before data collection. The present registration finalizes the analysis plan before any substantive data were inspected. The content analysis has been deferred to a separate paper because it would exceed the scope of the present study. The remaining refinements to the analysis plan, including the within-person/between-person decomposition of exposure, were made on methodological grounds and without knowledge of the results. This should therefore be considered a post-data-collection, pre-analysis registration.

live_data_statements: Before the field period, participants completed a screening questionnaire (consent, eligibility, demographics, social-media use, past-year gambling, and the PGSI) and received illustrated instructions that defined messages about gambling broadly, from operator advertising to memes, betting tips, and anti-gambling messages.
Participants were recruited through the commercial online panel IPSOS, the university participant pool, and flyers.
One further participant completed no scheduled questionnaire after the first one and was excluded.
Participants completed 1,976 of 2,314 possible questionnaires after the first (compliance rate of 85.4%; M = 11.10 per person, Mdn = 12, range 1-13).

We had preregistered a target of at least 180 analysable participants, based on simulations of the planned mixed models that assumed about 2.5 reported encounters per participant per day, an intraclass correlation of .40, a within-person coefficient of about 0.15 for positive expectancies and urge, and an odds ratio of about 1.40 for gambling; under these assumptions, 180 participants were expected to provide a power of at least .80.
Each scheduled questionnaire asked whether participants had gambled since the last notification and, if so, for how many minutes in total and with what total stake in euros.
Participants had to stop what they were doing, take a screenshot, and upload it.

text.text: Advertising restrictions largely remove gambling marketing from mass media, but digital channels, from social media to e-mail, leave room for paid, owned, and earned messages that are difficult to monitor.
In a seven-day ecological momentary assessment, 178 Dutch online gamblers aged 18-30 documented encounters with gambling marketing with a screenshot or photo; all 1,377 images were content-analysed.
At least one encounter was reported in 42% of assessment intervals and high-risk gamblers recalled more marketing encounters than other participants.

Half of the documented marketing came from Instagram or Facebook, half offered a financial inducement, and one in fourteen messages came from unlicensed operators or impersonated licensed brands; high-risk gamblers mostly documented operators' own posts, the other groups mostly paid ads.

At encounters, participants reported a stronger urge to gamble, anticipated more positive outcomes and more escalation of their gambling, and expected to feel less guilty about gambling than in their own unexposed moments.
Additionally, gambling was more likely in the same interval as an encounter.
Gambling marketing thus remains a routine part 2 of young gamblers' digital media use and encounters coincide with momentary shifts towards gambling.
A young adult who wants to place a bet today needs nothing more than a phone.
The same phone lets gambling operators reach that person at any moment: with an ad in their Instagram feed, a bonus offer by e-mail, or a text message about a free bet (De Jans et al., 2026).

text.text: In the Netherlands, where online gambling was legalized in 2021, young adults aged 18 to 23 held 22% of the online gambling accounts in use in the second half of 2025, although they make up only 9.3% of the adult population (Kansspelautoriteit, 2026b).

text.text: This overrepresentation is particularly concerning because young adults are especially vulnerable to gambling-related harms, with potentially lasting consequences for their future life prospects (Wardle et al., 2024).

text.text: Such harms include financial problems, emotional distress, reduced performance at work or study, and relationship conflict, and can occur even among people who do not meet diagnostic criteria for a gambling disorder (Langham et al., 2016; Wardle et al., 2024).

text.text: Current frameworks locate gambling harm not only in individuals but also in the commercial, technological, and social environments that make gambling available and attractive (Hilbrecht et al., 2020; Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Current frameworks locate gambling harm not only in individuals but also in the commercial, technological, and social environments that make gambling available and attractive <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hilbrecht et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Gambling marketing is part of this environment: it keeps gambling top of mind (Di Censo et al., 2024), links it to fun, sociability, and winning (Deans et al., 2016; Guillou-Landreat et al., 2021), and often places a route to participation, such as a "Bet here" link, next to the persuasive cue (Killick & Griffiths, 2020; Rossi & Nairn, 2022).

text.text: The Lancet Public Health Commission on gambling consequently recommends that governments prohibit or substantially restrict gambling advertising, sponsorship, and marketing (Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The Lancet Public Health Commission on gambling consequently recommends that governments prohibit or substantially restrict gambling advertising, sponsorship, and marketing <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Many countries have responded accordingly.
In the Netherlands, licensed online operators may no longer advertise on television or radio, in print, or in public spaces since July 2023, and sponsorship has been banned since July 2025.

Advertising online, by direct mail, on social media, and within the gambling environment remains permitted under conditions: recipients must be able to opt out, at least 95% of the audience reached must be aged 24 or older, and operators must keep minors, young adults, and people who show signs of risky gambling from being confronted with their advertising (Kansspelautoriteit, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

text.text: The channels that remain open differ from mass media in two respects.

First, the marketing forms available on social media platforms are not limited to paid ads: operators post on their own accounts, creators promote gambling to their followers (De Jans et al., 2026), and memes and videos carrying an operator's logo circulate in ways that may not be recognisable as marketing (Dighton et al., 2025; Rossi & Nairn, 2025), so the environment combines paid, owned, and earned media (Lovett & Staelin, 2016).

text.text: However, the public advertising repositories required by the EU Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Art. 39) cover only paid ads and thus solely show what was bought rather than what a given person encounters (Xiao & Deery, 2026).

text.text: Second, online marketing can be personalised on the basis of users' behaviour (Strycharz & Duivenvoorde, 2021).
text.formatted: Second, online marketing can be personalised on the basis of users' behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Strycharz & Duivenvoorde, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Engagement with gambling-related content may therefore lead to further marketing exposure, potentially concentrating repeated encounters among people already involved in gambling.
This could be particularly concerning for those experiencing gambling-related harm, as marketing may encourage unplanned spending in this group (Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This could be particularly concerning for those experiencing gambling-related harm, as marketing may encourage unplanned spending in this group <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore examined gambling marketing from the consumer's side.

In a seven-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA), Dutch online gamblers aged 18-30 documented encounters with a screenshot or photo, reported further encounters at twice-daily questionnaires, and rated their gambling expectancies and urge to gamble in every report and questionnaire.
The study makes three contributions.
First, it maps young gamblers' exposure to gambling marketing, documenting who encounters which forms of content and how often.
By capturing content that advertising repositories do not record, it provides policy-relevant evidence on the marketing that continues to reach young gamblers after restrictions on mass advertising.

Second, it examines momentary associations between marketing encounters and gambling expectancies, urges, and behaviour, connecting everyday exposure to the psychological and behavioural responses that accompany it.
Third, it provides a more differentiated account of susceptibility by examining gambling risk both as a predictor of exposure and as a moderator of momentary exposure-response associations.
Greater exposure does not necessarily imply stronger responses to individual encounters.

Separating these roles clarifies whether higher-risk gamblers' vulnerability is reflected in disproportionate marketing reach, heightened responsiveness, or both, with implications for where additional protection may be needed.
Reviews of gambling marketing link greater advertising exposure to increased gambling involvement, with evidence of a dose-response relationship (Bouguettaya et al., 2020; McGrane et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Reviews of gambling marketing link greater advertising exposure to increased gambling involvement, with evidence of a dose-response relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bouguettaya et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">McGrane et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, an overall dose-response pattern can coexist with substantial variation in how individuals respond to a given encounter.
Explaining this variation requires attention to the characteristics and experiences that users bring to media use.

The Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (DSMM; Valkenburg & Peter, 2013) holds that media effects are conditional: dispositional, developmental, and social characteristics shape which media people use and how strongly they respond.
text.formatted: The Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (DSMM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Valkenburg & Peter, 2013)</ref> holds that media effects are conditional: dispositional, developmental, and social characteristics shape which media people use and how strongly they respond.

text.text: Applied to gambling marketing, the DSMM points to two ways in which vulnerable people could be disadvantaged.
Under differential exposure, they encounter more marketing; under differential responsiveness, a comparable encounter affects them more.

These two paths correspond to the two roles the DSMM assigns to differential-susceptibility variables: they predict media use, and they moderate how strongly media use affects people's responses (Valkenburg & Peter, 2013).
text.formatted: These two paths correspond to the two roles the DSMM assigns to differential-susceptibility variables: they predict media use, and they moderate how strongly media use affects people's responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Valkenburg & Peter, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: We treat gambling risk as such a variable and examine both roles: its relation to exposure and its moderation of momentary responses.
Most evidence on gambling marketing rests on retrospective surveys in which people summarise weeks or months of exposure in a single judgement (Bouguettaya et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Most evidence on gambling marketing rests on retrospective surveys in which people summarise weeks or months of exposure in a single judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bouguettaya et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This work has shown a consistent link between exposure and gambling, but in cross-sectional data it is hard to tell whether marketing encourages gambling or simply reaches people who already gamble (Bouguettaya et al., 2020; Di Censo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This work has shown a consistent link between exposure and gambling, but in cross-sectional data it is hard to tell whether marketing encourages gambling or simply reaches people who already gamble <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bouguettaya et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Di Censo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Ecological momentary assessment studies address both problems by sampling experiences repeatedly, in daily life, and close to when they occur (Shiffman et al., 2008), which reduces recall bias and allows each person's exposed moments to be compared with their own unexposed moments (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013).
text.formatted: Ecological momentary assessment studies address both problems by sampling experiences repeatedly, in daily life, and close to when they occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Shiffman et al., 2008)</ref>, which reduces recall bias and allows each person's exposed moments to be compared with their own unexposed moments <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Ecological momentary assessment can capture exposure in two ways.

Event reports can be filed whenever an encounter occurs and can include screenshots or images of the message itself, but they require effort; scheduled reports ask about encounters not yet reported and demand less effort, but rely on memory.
Earlier ecological momentary assessment studies of gambling marketing largely relied on scheduled reports (Browne et al., 2019; Hing et al., 2025; Rockloff et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Earlier ecological momentary assessment studies of gambling marketing largely relied on scheduled reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Browne et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hing et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rockloff et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: De Jans et al. (2023) combined both reports: young adults in Flanders uploaded each gambling ad they encountered during one week, right away or in a daily survey that also recorded days without ads, and the uploads were content-analysed; participants encountered about six ads per week, mostly digital ones.
However, the study took place under Belgian rules that still allowed gambling advertising in most media.

After Belgium banned most gambling advertising in 2023, young people who gamble reported seeing less of it in qualitative interviews, but described what remained, such as e-mails, sponsored posts, and operators' own social media channels, as more targeted (De Jans et al., 2026).
text.formatted: After Belgium banned most gambling advertising in 2023, young people who gamble reported seeing less of it in qualitative interviews, but described what remained, such as e-mails, sponsored posts, and operators' own social media channels, as more targeted <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(De Jans et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For strongly regulated markets such as the gambling markets in Belgium and The Netherlands, three questions remain open.
How often do young adults still encounter gambling marketing?
Which media carry it: paid ads, or operators' own and earned channels that escape the repositories?
And where, from whom, and with what offers does it arrive?
These questions are pressing because the remaining channels are both hard to oversee and consequential due to personalization (De Jans et al., 2026; Strycharz & Duivenvoorde, 2021).
text.formatted: These questions are pressing because the remaining channels are both hard to oversee and consequential due to personalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(De Jans et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Strycharz & Duivenvoorde, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: RQ1: How often do young adults who gamble online encounter gambling marketing and what characterises the content?
Because gambling marketing remains permitted in digital and highly personalised environments, people who gamble regularly may encounter more of it.

People who gamble more often hold more online gambling accounts (Gainsbury et al., 2015), and some young people who gamble follow operators' social media channels to obtain bonuses and odds boosts (De Jans et al., 2026), which opens channels for direct communication and supplies signals for personalised delivery (Strycharz & Duivenvoorde, 2021).

text.text: Gambling cues may also be more salient to them, as gambling beliefs and gambling problems are linked to attentional biases for gambling cues (Grant & Bowling, 2015; McCusker & Gettings, 1997).

text.text: Accordingly, young people who gambled more often documented more gambling ads in Flanders (De Jans et al., 2023) and reported encountering more advertising after the Belgian ban (De Jans et al., 2026), and moderate-risk and problem gamblers more often recall gambling promotions on social media, engage with operators there (Gainsbury et al., 2016), and report more exposure to direct marketing (Syvertsen et al., 2022).

text.text: RQ2: Does exposure to gambling marketing and its characteristics differ by gambling risk?

Gambling marketing foregrounds winning, entertainment, and sociability (Deans et al., 2016; Guillou-Landreat et al., 2021), uses bonuses to make betting appear less costly or risky (Browne et al., 2019; McGrane et al., 2025; Rossi & Nairn, 2022), and provides direct routes to gambling (Killick & Griffiths, 2020).

text.text: Such framing may shape outcome expectancies, beliefs about consequences that guide behaviour (Bandura, 1986).
text.formatted: Such framing may shape outcome expectancies, beliefs about consequences that guide behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bandura, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Gambling expectancies comprise three positive dimensions (enjoyment, self-enhancement, and money) and two negative ones (over-involvement, or anticipated loss of control, and emotional impact, such as guilt; Gillespie et al., 2007).

text.text: Among adolescents, more positive expectancies are associated with more frequent gambling and gambling problems (Donati et al., 2022).

text.text: Another proximal outcome that positively framed gambling marketing is likely to influence is the urge to gamble, the subjectively experienced desire to gamble, which links expectancies to behaviour.
According to cue-reactivity research, cues repeatedly paired with gambling, such as brands, odds, and bonus offers, can come to elicit craving (Limbrick-Oldfield et al., 2017).
text.formatted: According to cue-reactivity research, cues repeatedly paired with gambling, such as brands, odds, and bonus offers, can come to elicit craving <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Limbrick-Oldfield et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In daily life, momentary cravings predicted gambling episodes (Hawker et al., 2021), and craving is linked to gambling severity and loss chasing (Mallorquí-Bagué et al., 2023).

text.text: If marketing encounters shift expectancies and urge, the question is whether they are also followed by gambling, as momentary cravings preceded gambling episodes in daily life (Hawker et al., 2021).

text.text: In Australian ecological momentary assessment studies, operator e-mails and text messages were followed by betting intentions and betting (Russell et al., 2018), advertisements and inducements by higher intended and actual expenditure (Browne et al., 2019), and direct messages from operators, tipsters, and affiliates by more betting, expenditure, and harm (Hing et al., 2025).

text.text: These studies concerned wagering and relied on recalled encounters, and consequently, they were not able to capture how people felt at the moment of an encounter.
In contrast to whether and how much someone bet, momentary states are harder to recall afterwards (Shiffman et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In contrast to whether and how much someone bet, momentary states are harder to recall afterwards <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Shiffman et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Research on the marketing of other health-relevant products, alcohol and food, shows how such states can be captured.

Participants filed a short report whenever they saw an ad and answered the same questions at random prompts, so that each person's states at exposure could be compared with their own states at other moments (Boyland et al., 2024; Martino et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Participants filed a short report whenever they saw an ad and answered the same questions at random prompts, so that each person's states at exposure could be compared with their own states at other moments <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Boyland et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Martino et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We applied this design to gambling marketing: event reports document the message and capture states at the encounter, scheduled questionnaires add encounters that could not be documented, and each participant's exposed moments are compared with their own unexposed ones.

H1: At encounters with gambling marketing, participants report more positive gambling expectancies (H1a), less negative gambling expectancies (H1b), and stronger urge (H1c) than in their own unexposed moments, and they are more likely to gamble in the same interval as an encounter (H1d).
In the DSMM, susceptibility factors can stimulate or reduce media effects (Valkenburg & Peter, 2013); for gambling risk, cue-reactivity research points to stronger responses.
text.formatted: In the DSMM, susceptibility factors can stimulate or reduce media effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Valkenburg & Peter, 2013)</ref>; for gambling risk, cue-reactivity research points to stronger responses.

text.text: Through repeated gambling, brands, bonuses, and odds can acquire learned associations with reward.

People with behavioural addictions, including gambling disorder, report stronger subjective reactions to addiction-related cues than controls (Starcke et al., 2018), and people with gambling disorder show stronger reward-related brain responses to gambling cues (Limbrick-Oldfield et al., 2017).

text.text: Operators' direct messages predicted betting, spending, and harm particularly strongly among higher-risk bettors (Hing et al., 2025).

text.text: People with more severe problems also report stronger perceived advertising effects (Binde & Romild, 2019; Hanss et al., 2015; Syvertsen et al., 2022), but these are self-assessments of influence rather than observed responses.

text.text: A withinperson test comes closer to responsiveness: a larger difference between a person's exposed and unexposed moments at higher risk indicates a stronger response rather than more exposure.
H2: The differences proposed in H1 are stronger in higher PGSI risk categories for positive expectancies (H2a), negative expectancies (H2b), urge (H2c), and gambling (H2d).
To capture the exposure and proximal responses to gambling marketing, we conducted a seven-day ecological momentary assessment using the Avicenna software and application.

Each day, participants received a morning questionnaire (at a random time between 8:00 a.m. and noon) and an evening questionnaire (at a random time between 4:00 and 8:00 p.m.), 14 in total; the first marked the start of the first assessment interval.
These scheduled questionnaires counted as valid when completed within 120 minutes of the prompt.

Because each interval ran from one questionnaire to the next, daytime intervals (morning to evening) were shorter than overnight intervals; all interval-level models therefore adjusted for interval length.
Data were collected between January and September 2026.
Our reporting follows the Checklist for Reporting Ecological Momentary Assessment Studies (CREMAS; Liao et al., 2016).

text.text: Before the field period, participants completed a screening questionnaire (consent, eligibility, demographics, social-media use, past-year gambling, and the PGSI) and received illustrated instructions that defined messages about gambling broadly, from operator advertising to memes, betting tips, and anti-gambling messages.

Whenever participants saw or heard such a message, they were asked to file an event report immediately or at the latest within 60 minutes, rate their current expectancies and urge, and upload a screenshot or photo.
We chose this limit because event-contingent reports should be close to the event (Shiffman et al., 2008) as urges rise quickly after cues and peaks together with them (Gauld et al., 2025).

text.text: At each scheduled questionnaire, participants rated their expectancies and urge and reported whether they had gambled since the last notification and any encounter not yet reported, including when the most recent one had occurred and what kind of message it was.
Compensation (maximum €50) covered completed questionnaires and up to three event reports per day, a cap intended to discourage searching for gambling messages.
Contact details of the support service Open over Gokken appeared in every questionnaire.
The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of [blinded for review] (FMG-17175), and it was preregistered on AsPredicted before data analysis (https://aspredicted.org/wc4vk4.pdf).

text.text: Participants were recruited through the commercial online panel IPSOS, the university participant pool, and flyers.
Eligible were residents of the Netherlands aged 18-30 who bet on sports online or gambled online in another form at least once every six months.

Of 205 participants who passed the screening and completed the first scheduled questionnaire, we later identified 26 enrolments that probably repeated an earlier enrolment by the same person, because they had been made on a device already used for another enrolment; we kept only the earliest enrolment per device.
One further participant completed no scheduled questionnaire after the first one and was excluded.
The final analytic sample thus comprised 178 participants aged 18-30 (M = 24.20, SD = 3.68); 109 identified as men, 68 as women, and one as nonbinary.
In the past year, 87.1% had bet on sports online and 78.7% had played online casino games.
Participants completed 1,976 of 2,314 possible questionnaires after the first (compliance rate of 85.4%; M = 11.10 per person, Mdn = 12, range 1-13).

We had preregistered a target of at least 180 analysable participants, based on simulations of the planned mixed models that assumed about 2.5 reported encounters per participant per day, an intraclass correlation of .40, a within-person coefficient of about 0.15 for positive expectancies and urge, and an odds ratio of about 1.40 for gambling; under these assumptions, 180 participants were expected to provide a power of at least .80.
Interactions with risk were not powered.

The final sample fell slightly short of this target, and exposure was lower than assumed (about one documented encounter per participant per day rather than 2.5), which reduces the power of the within-person comparisons.
Event reports were retained when the encounter had occurred no more than 60 minutes before submission and were assigned to the interval in which they occurred.

A report counted as an encounter with gambling marketing when the image coding showed paid, owned, or earned marketing (Lovett & Staelin, 2016): advertising placed by or for a gambling operator (paid), operators' own posts, websites, and direct messages (owned), or undisclosed creator or meme content showing an operator brand (earned; Dighton et al., 2025; Rossi & Nairn, 2025).

text.text: Services around gambling, such as tipster apps, generic gambling content, prevention messages, and unrelated images did not count.

Encounters reported at scheduled questionnaires counted as marketing when participants described the message as promoting gambling or offering promotions or extras, the closest match available for encounters without an image.
At the interval level, exposure was coded as documented (at least one counted event report), recalled (a promotional encounter reported at the scheduled questionnaire), or any (either or both).

For the analyses of momentary states, an encounter was either an event report or a scheduled questionnaire at which participants reported a recalled promotional encounter within the preceding 60 minutes.
All 1,377 images attached to retained event reports were content-analysed with a codebook developed for this study (Krippendorff, 2018; Neuendorf, 2017).

text.text: Each image first received one of five codes: paid or owned gambling marketing, commercial service around gambling, other gambling content (flagged when it showed an operator brand), prevention, or not gambling-related.

Paid and owned marketing was further coded for product, source (e.g., labelled paid ad, operator's own post, direct message, affiliate, sponsorship), inducement (financial, competition, gift, or none), platform, and brand, following the visible content only.

From the source we derived the media type: paid (labelled ads, affiliates, disclosed creator content, sponsorship, offline advertising), owned (operators' own posts, websites, direct messages), or earned (other gambling content with an operator brand).
Licence status was derived from the brand using the register of the Dutch Gambling Authority.
The first coding of all images was carried out with a locally-run large language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5, Anthropic) provided by our university to ensure compliance with local privacy regulations.
Such LLMs can match human annotators in many annotation tasks (Gilardi et al., 2023; Rathje et al., 2024) but must be validated for each task (Törnberg, 2024).

The nine PGSI items (0 = never to3 = almost always) were summed (range 0-27; M = 5.71, SD = 6.17, Mdn = 3).

text.text: The first three are positive expectancies (enjoyment, self-enhancement, and money), the last two negative expectancies (escalation and guilt).
The three positive items were averaged into a composite of positive expectancies (α = .88 between persons, .61 within persons).
The two negative items were barely related within persons (r = -.08) and were analysed separately.
Urge was measured with "How would you rate your desire to gamble at this moment?"

text.text: Each scheduled questionnaire asked whether participants had gambled since the last notification and, if so, for how many minutes in total and with what total stake in euros.

Eightyeight participants reported gambling in 388 intervals (19.6%); episodes lasted on average 37.7 minutes (SD = 39.8, Mdn = 30, range 0-350) with an average stake of €30.74 (SD = 34.9, Mdn = 20, range 0-300).
RQ1 was addressed descriptively.

For RQ2, we fitted logistic mixed models with participant random intercepts for documented, recalled, and any exposure, testing the four risk categories jointly (likelihood-ratio test, 3 df) and against the no-risk group.

To compare what the four groups documented, we fitted the same models at the image level for media type (paid, owned, earned), platform type (social media; e-mail or text message), financial inducement, and unlicensed or impersonating ads.

For H1a to H1c, we compared states at encounters with the same participant's states at scheduled questionnaires from intervals without any reported encounter, using linear mixed models with a person-mean-centred encounter indicator, the participant's mean, and random intercepts and encounter slopes (Curran & Bauer, 2011).

text.text: Because event reports were spread across the day, models adjusted for part of the day and weekend.
For H1d, we fitted logistic mixed models with person-mean-centred exposure for gambling in the same interval and, among intervals with gambling, linear mixed models of log-transformed time and stake.
Interval-level models (RQ2, H1d) adjusted for questionnaire time (morning or evening), study day, weekend, interval length, and the final questionnaire.
For H2, we added encounter × risk-category interactions (likelihood-ratio tests, 3 df).

We applied Holm's procedure (Holm, 1979) where several tests addressed one hypothesis or question that a single significant result would support (Rubin, 2021): across the two negative expectancy items (H1b, H2b), the three comparisons with the no-risk group, and the seven marketing characteristics.

text.text: Paid media made up 88.1% of the marketing documented by no-risk participants but only 27.0% of that documented by high-risk participants, whereas owned media rose from 10.3% to 58.4%, mostly operators' Instagram posts.

Owned posts reach people who follow an operator, which fits the idea that gambling involvement opens owned channels (De Jans et al., 2026; Gainsbury et al., 2016); the marketing reaching the group the rules are meant to protect is thus largely the part that advertising repositories do not record.

text.text: High-risk participants also documented fewer messages with a financial inducement.
Earned media, direct messages, and unlicensed or impersonating ads did not differ reliably by risk, but these tests had little power.

The analysis of states (Table 4) compared 1,439 encounters (1,190 documented, 249 recalled within 60 minutes) with 1,021 scheduled questionnaires from intervals without an encounter; because each participant served as their own comparison, the encounter effects rest on the 154 of 178 participants who reported at least one encounter.

text.text: At encounters, participants anticipated slightly more positive outcomes of gambling than in their unexposed moments (b = 0.09, 95% CI [0.00, 0.17], p = .047), supporting H1a.
As predicted, they expected to feel less guilty if they gambled (b = -0.17, Holm p = .025), but, contrary to H1b, they also anticipated more escalation of their gambling (b = 0.17, Holm p = .011).
Urge was about three and a half points higher on the 100-point scale (b = 3.40, p < .001), supporting H1c.

text.text: Encounters made gambling seem slightly more rewarding, in line with marketing that foregrounds winning, entertainment, and sociability (Deans et al., 2016; Guillou-Landreat et al., 2021).

text.text: The difference was small (d = 0.14), and the lower bound of its confidence interval was close to zero, although positive expectancies had room to rise (M = 3.13 on the 7-point scale at scheduled questionnaires).
The negative expectancies shifted as well, but these shifts allow several readings.
Lower anticipated guilt could reflect normalisation, as sponsored gambling posts made young adults think that a typical student gambles more often (Hartmann et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Lower anticipated guilt could reflect normalisation, as sponsored gambling posts made young adults think that a typical student gambles more often <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hartmann et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Higher anticipated escalation may mean that encounters made further gambling more tempting.
The difference in urge fits cue-reactivity research (Limbrick-Oldfield et al., 2017; Starcke et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The difference in urge fits cue-reactivity research <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Limbrick-Oldfield et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Starcke et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The effect is small however (d = 0.25), and whether such momentary differences add up across frequent encounters, or translate into gambling as momentary cravings did in earlier ecological momentary assessment research (Hawker et al., 2021), remains to be tested.

text.text: Gambling was more likely in intervals with an encounter than in the same participant's unexposed intervals (OR = 1.97, 95% CI [1.27, 3.06], p = .003), supporting H1d and in line with Australian ecological momentary assessment studies (Browne et al., 2019; Hing et al., 2025; Russell et al., 2018), although participants did not gamble longer (-0.4%, 95% CI [-17.8, 20.7]) or stake more (-9.5%, 95% CI [-31.3, 19.2]) when they gambled.

text.text: Slightly more positive expectancies, a stronger urge, and more anticipated escalation could make gambling more likely when an opportunity arises (Bandura, 1986; Hawker et al., 2021; Hofmann et al., 2012).

text.text: Our design, however, shows co-occurrence, not causation.
The order of encounters and gambling within an interval is unknown.
Experiments could test causality: when Rockloff et al. (2026) randomised participants to opt out of operators' direct marketing, they placed fewer bets, spent less, and reported fewer harms.

text.text: Gambling risk did not moderate the differences in positive expectancies (H2a), χ²(3) = 0.19, p = .979, anticipated escalation (H2b), χ²(3) = 3.10, Holm p = .376, urge (H2c), χ²(3) = 1.47, p = .690, the likelihood of gambling (H2d), χ²(3) = 7.26, p = .064, or gambling time, χ²(3) = 2.11, p = .549.

It did moderate anticipated guilt, χ²(3) = 10.38, Holm p = .031, and stake, χ²(3) = 8.86, p = .031, in both cases only in the low-risk group, with lower anticipated guilt at encounters (b = -0.58, 95% CI [-1.02, -0.14]; other groups b = -0.05 to 0.01) and higher stakes in exposed intervals (+422%, 95% CI [35, 1, 914]; 34 gambling intervals from 16 participants).

text.text: None of these patterns followed a risk gradient, so H2 was not supported.

Surveys in which people with gambling problems report stronger advertising effects (Binde & Romild, 2019; Hanss et al., 2015; Syvertsen et al., 2022) capture perceived impact, whereas we tested whether the same person's response to an encounter was larger at higher risk.

text.text: The low-risk pattern for guilt was not predicted and needs replication; it may partly reflect that no-risk participants anticipated little guilt in the first place (M = 2.91 vs.
4.10 to 4.40 in the other groups).

The null results are not evidence of equal susceptibility: with 33 to 54 participants per risk category and about one documented encounter per person per day, only large differences in responsiveness could have been detected.
We set out to separate two ways in which gambling marketing could disadvantage people at higher gambling risk: encountering more of it and responding more strongly to it (Valkenburg & Peter, 2013).
text.formatted: We set out to separate two ways in which gambling marketing could disadvantage people at higher gambling risk: encountering more of it and responding more strongly to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Valkenburg & Peter, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings point to the first.

High-risk gamblers did not document more marketing than other participants, but they recalled far more encounters, most of their gambling intervals contained one, and what they documented came mostly from operators' own accounts.

Their momentary responses, in contrast, were not larger: encounters coincided with a stronger urge, slightly more positive expectancies, and more anticipated escalation, and these differences did not grow with gambling risk, although only large differences in responsiveness could have been detected.

In a market that has restricted mass advertising, gambling risk thus seems to matter mainly for how often and through which channels marketing arrives, and these are the channels that are hardest to monitor.
For regulators, these findings highlight the need to monitor the marketing young adults actually encounter.
Advertising repositories capture paid advertisements but leave out unpaid posts from operators' accounts and private promotional messages.
Participant screenshots, combined where possible with platform data donated with consent, could help capture these encounters (Araujo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Participant screenshots, combined where possible with platform data donated with consent, could help capture these encounters <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Araujo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Compliance checks should therefore include operators' own accounts and marketing within betting apps and websites.
Existing research using Meta's advertising repository provides a starting point for examining age-targeting and audience reach (Xiao & Deery, 2026).
text.formatted: Existing research using Meta's advertising repository provides a starting point for examining age-targeting and audience reach <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Xiao & Deery, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such audits should assess whether at least 95% of the audience reached by online gambling advertising is aged 24 or older.
Targeted protections for people showing signs of risky gambling remain important (Kansspelautoriteit, n.d.-b).
text.formatted: Targeted protections for people showing signs of risky gambling remain important <ref type="bibr">(Kansspelautoriteit, n.d.-b)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings also caution against assuming that only high-risk gamblers respond to marketing.
Marketing encounters were associated with momentary shifts in the sample as a whole, although differences in responsiveness between risk groups could not be estimated precisely.
Targeted safeguards should therefore complement broader restrictions on marketing exposure, as recommended by the Lancet Public Health Commission (Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Targeted safeguards should therefore complement broader restrictions on marketing exposure, as recommended by the Lancet Public Health Commission <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Several limitations should be considered.
First, exposure measurement depended on participants noticing, recognising, and reporting gambling marketing.
Screenshots allowed verification of content, but only for encounters participants documented.
Individual differences in attention to gambling cues (Grant & Bowling, 2015) may also influence which encounters are remembered and reported.
text.formatted: Individual differences in attention to gambling cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Grant & Bowling, 2015)</ref> may also influence which encounters are remembered and reported.

text.text: Consequently, differences in reported exposure may reflect both differences in marketing encounters and differences in attention, recall, or documentation.

Future studies could combine documented and recalled encounters with passive capture or data donation, where suitable exposure records are available, to reduce documentation demands (Araujo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Future studies could combine documented and recalled encounters with passive capture or data donation, where suitable exposure records are available, to reduce documentation demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Araujo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the order of marketing encounters, gambling, and momentary states within each reporting interval was unknown.
Participants may have noticed or reported more marketing because they were already gambling or considering gambling.
The observed associations therefore cannot establish whether exposure preceded changes in expectancies, urges, or behaviour.
Combining time-stamped gambling records with passively captured exposure could clarify temporal order, while experiments could provide evidence about causal effects.
Third, fewer participants and documented encounters were available than planned.
We excluded 26 probable repeat enrolments, and participants documented approximately one encounter per day rather than the expected 2.5.
This limited the information available for withinperson comparisons, particularly analyses of differences by gambling risk.
Future studies should anticipate lower documentation rates when planning sample sizes and assessment periods.
Future research should also distinguish paid, owned, and earned media (Lovett & Staelin, 2016).
text.formatted: Future research should also distinguish paid, owned, and earned media <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lovett & Staelin, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Operators' own accounts were the source of most marketing documented by high-risk participants in this study.
Measures limited to paid-advertising repositories would miss unpaid content from these accounts, underlining the importance of capturing exposure across different marketing channels.
Advertising restrictions aim to protect people from gambling marketing, and those most at risk above all.

Among young Dutch adults who gamble online, gambling marketing remained part of everyday media, half of it on Instagram and Facebook, often with financial inducements, and sometimes from unlicensed operators or impersonators.

Encounters coincided with a stronger urge, slightly more positive expectancies, and more anticipated escalation, and these shifts did not grow with gambling risk; high-risk gamblers instead reported more exposure, much of it from operators' own accounts.
Judging whether restrictions achieve their aim requires monitoring the owned, earned, and direct messages that advertising repositories do not document.
